subsections.title: Overview
subsections.summary: Chapter 6 gives step-by-step procedures for designing soil nail walls. A project runs through four phases: initial design considerations, design, pre-construction, and construction and post-construction; Tables 6.1 and 6.2 list the steps and sub-steps. The Design phase is the focus; the other three are introduced for completeness. The sequence does not depend on who designs: it applies to Design/Bid/Build and approximately to Design/Build.
subsections.body: 6.1.1 Overview (pp. 143-145). This chapter presents step-by-step procedures for the design of soil nail walls. The principal activities take place in four main phases: initial design considerations; design; pre-construction; and construction and post-construction. The sequence of the major steps and sub-steps is listed in Table 6.1 (Steps 1 to 3: Step 1 Project Requirements, with sub-steps a to c; Step 2 Subsurface Exploration and Development of Parameters for Design, a to g; Step 3 Load Definition, a and b) and Table 6.2 (Steps 4 to 12, from Step 4 Soil-Nail Configuration and Material Selection to Step 12 Preparation of Construction Drawings and Specifications). The Design phase is the focus of the chapter; the other three phases are introduced for completeness and only briefly discussed. The sequence of work in Tables 6.1 and 6.2 is independent of who does the design: it applies when an Owner (typically a public agency) or the Owner's consultant performs the analysis, design and plan preparation in a Design/Bid/Build contract, and should be approximately the same if the Owner procures the project as a Design/Build contract; the difference is the proportion of design work performed by the Owner's and the Contractor's design teams.

subsections.title: Initial Design Considerations
subsections.summary: Initial design considerations: Step 1, the Owner sets project requirements, standards, performance and assembles existing geotechnical information; Step 2, subsurface exploration and design parameters, plus corrosion protection level, preliminary layouts, preliminary overall stability and basal heave, deformation criteria near sensitive structures (strict limits under about 0.5 in. may favor a soldier pile anchor or secant pile wall) and a risk evaluation; Step 3, loads combined per AASHTO (2012) for Strength I, Service I and Extreme Event I.
subsections.body: 6.1.2 Initial Design Considerations (pp. 145-146). This phase establishes the project performance requirements and constraints (Step 1), collects geotechnical information (Step 2) and defines loads (Step 3). Step 1 Project Requirements: the Owner must establish or confirm the project requirements and constraints, confirm the design standards, select the expected project performance (critical or not, permanent or not), and collect and assemble the preliminary geotechnical information that exists. Step 2 Subsurface Exploration and Development of Parameters for Design: the Owner performs or commissions the preliminary evaluations to establish baselines, develop criteria in specifications and evaluate feasibility and constructability. A thorough understanding of the geotechnical conditions is of utmost importance; the characterization of site variability, the soil design parameters and the site corrosion and frost potentials need to be completed before the Design phase starts. The Owner should also select the level of corrosion protection of the soil nails, develop preliminary plan layouts, and perform preliminary overall stability and basal heave analyses; if a sensitive structure exists next to the planned excavation, the Owner is expected to define the performance criteria and perform a preliminary deformation evaluation. If the Owner has strict limits for deformation (less than approximately 0.5 in.), a soldier pile anchor wall or a secant pile wall may be considered; publications on top-down excavation performance (e.g., Clough and O'Rourke 1990) may help. The required corrosion protection level is determined from soil corrosion test results and the selection procedures of Chapter 7 (solid bars) and Chapter 10 (HBSNs). Preliminary deformation analyses help identify problem areas and measures to limit displacements; where deformations are of concern the project documents must include monitoring requirements. Owners must also conduct a risk evaluation (right-of-way constraints, traffic control and phasing, schedule, access restrictions, subsurface hazards, seismic exposure) and determine the wall face aesthetic requirements and the procurement method; the engineer should consider all aspects that affect constructability (access, overhead limitations, obstructions, soil type, drainage, traffic). Step 3 Load Definition: the engineer defines the permanent, transient and extreme-event loads (Chapter 5) and determines load combinations according to AASHTO (2012); for highway soil nail walls the combinations are generally applicable to the Strength I, Service I and Extreme-Event I (earthquake) limit states.

subsections.title: Introduction
subsections.summary: Step 4 starts from the geometric constraints: the engineer sets preliminary cross sections (number of nails, vertical and horizontal spacing, inclination and length), all expected to be adjusted as design progresses, establishes corrosion protection features for the selected protection level (detailed in Step 4e), and selects a soil nail type and its mechanical properties before verifying the strength limit states.
subsections.body: 6.3.1 Introduction (p. 147). Once the existing geometric constraints are identified, the engineer must establish preliminary wall cross sections, including the number of nails, vertical and horizontal nail spacing, and nail inclination and length; all of these are expected to be adjusted to some degree as the design progresses. At this stage the engineer should evaluate the corrosion protection requirements and establish the corrosion protection features that meet the selected level of protection (details can be defined later, in Step 4e). Finally, the engineer must select a soil nail type and its mechanical properties before starting the verification of strength limit states.

Constructability issues may include obstructions encountered during a pre-construction site survey, limitations specific to the drilling equipment, and potential cost-saving and construction scheduling adjustments.

subsections.title: Step 4b Develop Soil Nail Wall Cross Sections
subsections.summary: Step 4b sets the cross section: batter (a moderate batter up to about 10 degrees reduces nail forces), spacing (4 to 6 ft, occasionally 6.5 ft, routinely 5 ft; SH x SV less than about 36 to 42 ft2; first row no deeper than about 2 to 3.5 ft; minimum about 3.5 ft), inclination (10 to 20 degrees, most commonly 15; avoid less than 10), length (about 0.7H to start; above about 1.2H suggests unfavorable ground) and the distribution of lengths in elevation (Byrne et al. 1996).
subsections.body: 6.3.3 Step 4b Develop Soil Nail Wall Cross Sections (pp. 147-153). Wall Batter (6.3.3a, p. 147): the batter is selected considering design, cost and aesthetics. The face can be vertical or nearly vertical; a moderate (up to about 10 degrees) batter reduces the forces transferred to the nails and allows shorter nails. A larger batter can contribute to face stability, may eliminate temporary berms in unstable sections and allow nailing in less advantageous soils, but the savings in shorter nails can be partly offset by the larger face area and excavation volume. A mild batter may help aesthetics, especially around horizontal curves; truly vertical walls often appear to lean inward. Soil Nail Spacing (6.3.3b, p. 148): nails are installed in a grid; SH is often the same as SV (Figure 6.1). Spacing in both directions generally ranges from 4 to 6 ft, occasionally up to 6.5 ft, and is routinely 5 ft; SH x SV can be checked to be less than approximately 36 to 42 ft2. The first row should not be deeper than approximately 2 to 3.5 ft from the top edge of the wall (instability of the upper lift, cantilever effects on the temporary facing), and the lowermost row about 2 to 3 ft above the base of the excavation; these limits may be adjusted for project conditions based on suitable analysis. Uniform spacing simplifies construction and quality control, but spacing must be adjusted near the top and bottom of walls, where the grade changes, at wall corners and ends (Figure 6.2a) and around utilities; it is commonly more practical to install the upper nails in one or two rows parallel or sub-parallel to the top of the wall and the others in between, at a maximum spacing of approximately 6 ft. A minimum spacing of approximately 3.5 ft reduces the potential for drilling into installed nails; close spacing may also overlap stresses as with closely spaced piles; exceptions may arise under concentrated loads such as existing foundations. Soil Nail Inclination (6.3.3c, p. 150): nails are installed at 10 to 20 degrees from horizontal, most commonly 15 degrees, at which grout flows from the bottom of the hole to the head without air pockets. Inclinations less than 10 degrees should be avoided (voids in the grout and an extended bird's beak at the head reduce pullout resistance and corrosion protection). Nails may need to be steeper around utilities or underground structures (Figure 6.2b), which affect only the upper rows; nails should not be installed above utilities because future excavations for maintenance will likely disturb the wall. Steeper nails can reach competent soils near the base, but too steep a direction cancels the benefit; nails steeper than about 40 to 45 degrees may be in compression. Overhead restrictions under existing bridges may force shallow inclinations of the first rows or a facing reinforced for cantilevers taller than 3.5 ft, and narrow deep excavations may force steeper nails. Steep nails need a vertical reaction from the facing that soil nail programs do not calculate (Section 6.10.3). Soil Nail Length (6.3.3d, pp. 151-152): for a preliminary section the length can be estimated as approximately 0.7H (H the wall height); longer nails are needed in weak soils, where deep-seated critical slip surfaces exist, with large surcharge loads, or with a rising backslope. A batter of 10 percent reduces the length requirement by approximately 10 to 15 percent compared with a vertical face. Lengths greater than about 1.2H, found with well-selected parameters and appropriate analysis, may suggest that ground conditions are not favorable for soil nailing; lengths less than 0.5H will not likely satisfy sliding stability, and lengths less than approximately 0.6H are rare. Distribution of Soil Nail Lengths in Elevation (6.3.3e, pp. 152-153): uniform lengths are common, but limit-equilibrium programs then predict the largest forces in the lower part of the wall, whereas measured forces are largest in the upper two thirds (Section 5.6.2), and the load distribution is inefficient; a uniform pattern is not unsafe but not optimal for limiting deformation. Shorter nails in the lower half (with longer upper rows for the same factor of safety) give smaller Tmax, a better load distribution and smaller movements. Guidelines based on Byrne et al. (1996): nails with heads in the upper half have a uniform length L; in the lower half, lengths are interpolated linearly from L at mid-height to R x L at the base, with 0.15 <= R <= 0.30 for very dense, coarse-grained granular soils, 0.25 <= R <= 0.40 for silty sand, sand to gravelly sand, and 0.30 <= R <= 0.45 for fine-grained soils. R was estimated for FSPO = 2.0, DDH 4 to 8 in., SH and SV 4 to 6 ft, typical bond strengths, soil unit weight 110 to 130 pcf and L/H 0.75 to 1.0; larger DDH and qu with smaller SH, SV and unit weight give lower R. SNAP-2 can make such a correction if the user selects it (it is not a default). Other patterns (longest in the upper third, intermediate in the central third, shortest in the lower third) also lower Tmax and deflections, and utilities may require some nails longer to compensate for others shorter; stability analyses must verify any pattern.
key_points: Moderate batter (up to about 10 degrees) reduces nail forces and allows shorter nails; truly vertical walls appear to lean inward
Spacing 4 to 6 ft (occasionally 6.5 ft), routinely 5 ft; SH x SV less than about 36 to 42 ft2; minimum about 3.5 ft; maximum about 6 ft between rows
First row no deeper than about 2 to 3.5 ft below the top; lowest row about 2 to 3 ft above the excavation base
Inclination 10 to 20 degrees, most commonly 15; avoid less than 10; nails steeper than about 40 to 45 degrees may be in compression
No nails above utilities; overhead restrictions may force shallow upper nails or facing reinforced for cantilevers over 3.5 ft
Preliminary length about 0.7H; above about 1.2H suggests unfavorable ground; below 0.5H unlikely to satisfy sliding; below about 0.6H rare
A 10 percent batter reduces nail length by about 10 to 15 percent
Lower-half nails shortened linearly to R x L at the base: R 0.15-0.30 dense coarse-grained, 0.25-0.40 sands, 0.30-0.45 fine-grained (Byrne et al. 1996)

subsections.title: Step 4c Select Soil Nail Pattern on Wall Face
subsections.summary: Step 4c: nails are installed in square or, more commonly, staggered (triangular or offset) patterns (Figure 6.1), irregular where space is restricted. The square pattern eases vertical shotcrete joints and precast panels and keeps drain strips equidistant from nails; the staggered pattern gives more uniform earth pressures, better arching and slightly larger resistance.
subsections.body: 6.3.4 Step 4c Select Soil Nail Pattern on Wall Face (p. 154). Soil nails are installed on the excavation face in square or, more commonly, staggered (also referred to as triangular or offset) patterns (Figure 6.1); the pattern can become irregular at locations with space restrictions. In the square pattern nails are vertically aligned in rows, which allows easy construction of vertical joints in shotcrete and easier installation of precast concrete panels (if used), and drain strips are equidistant from the nails. A staggered pattern results in more uniform earth-pressure distributions and better soil arching, and provides slightly larger resistance than a square pattern.
key_points: Staggered (triangular, offset) pattern more common than square (Figure 6.1)
Square pattern: easy vertical shotcrete joints and precast panels; drain strips equidistant from nails
Staggered pattern: more uniform earth pressures, better arching, slightly larger resistance

subsections.title: Step 4d Evaluate Soil Nail Horizontal Splaying
subsections.summary: Step 4d: nails may be splayed in plan to avoid manholes and other obstructions, to avoid interference at external corners (Figure 6.2c), or possibly to improve stability at internal corners. Splaying must be considered before using a design program, because the programs do not account for the splay angle.
subsections.body: 6.3.5 Step 4d Evaluate Soil Nail Horizontal Splaying (p. 154). Nails may need to be splayed in plan view to: (i) avoid manholes and other obstructions; (ii) avoid external corners, because of interference with adjacent nails (Figure 6.2c); or (iii) possibly improve stability at internal corners. The engineer must consider nail splaying before using a design computer program, because these programs do not account for the splay angle.
key_points: Splay nails to avoid obstructions and interference at external corners (Figure 6.2c)
Design programs do not account for the splay angle

subsections.title: Step 4f Select Soil Nail Type and Material Properties
subsections.summary: Step 4f: the engineer selects the steel grade for the soil nail bar and other metallic parts (Chapter 3, Appendix A). In Design/Bid/Build the engineer may estimate a practical minimum drill hole diameter for the bond resistance, but the Contractor ultimately selects the diameter to obtain the specified nominal pullout resistance and to allow cleaning, a tremie pipe, couplers and centralizers.
subsections.body: 6.3.7 Step 4f Select Soil Nail Type and Material Properties (p. 154). The engineer must select a grade of steel for the soil nail bar and other metallic parts; steel grades and sizes are in Chapter 3 and Appendix A. In traditional Design/Bid/Build contracts the engineer may estimate a practical minimum drill hole diameter to provide the bond resistance required for stability; however, the drill hole diameter is ultimately selected by the Contractor to obtain the specified nominal pullout resistance and possibly to allow cleaning the drill hole or accommodating a tremie pipe, tendon couplers and centralizers.

subsections.title: Step 6a Evaluate Internal Stability
subsections.summary: Step 6a: internal stability by 2D limit-equilibrium ASD slope stability analysis, preferably with a well-established soil nail program. The program gives FSOS and the nail loads; Tmax, the largest, is used in the LRFD checks. Minimum FSOS (Table 5.1): 1.5 critical and 1.35 non-critical permanent walls (static); 1.30 and 1.20 (printed '120') for temporary excavation; 1.1 seismic, or 1.0 when kh is based on allowable deformations. Nail lengths are iterated; too-long nails call for a larger hole or closer spacing.
subsections.body: 6.5.1 Step 6a Evaluate Internal Stability (pp. 156-158). Internal stability is typically analyzed with two-dimensional, limit-equilibrium, ASD-based slope stability procedures in readily available programs; a well-established soil nail program that can model multiple strata, groundwater, external and seismic loads and various geometric features should be preferred. The program calculates the overall factor of safety FSOS and the maximum loads of all nails (limited by tensile, pullout or facing resistances); the maximum among all nails, Tmax, is selected for the LRFD verifications. Uniform nail lengths give larger Tmax than nails increasingly shorter toward the base, for the same FSOS. The engineer enters bond strengths for each representative layer (printed as developed in Step 3e), wall geometry, nail layout, groundwater and external loads (Steps 4a-4d), with soil parameters characterized per Chapter 4 (unit weight, effective cohesion, effective friction angle, bond strength); preferably mean values. Minimum FSOS for internal stability (Table 5.1): static, permanent, critical 1.5; static, permanent, non-critical 1.35 (also for a critical structure when design uncertainty is limited, e.g., abundant geotechnical information and successful local experience); static, temporary excavation (lifts unsupported for up to 2 days) for critical permanent structures 1.30, and for non-critical ones printed '120' (1.20); seismic, when permanent seismic deformations are not taken into account, 1.1; seismic, when kh is based on estimated allowable seismic deformations, 1.0. Some ASD programs require factors of safety or reduction factors for pullout, tension and facing flexure (minimums in Table 5.1); the ultimate tensile and facing punching resistances are estimated outside the program (Table 6.3 or Step 7) using mean strengths; SNAP-2 calculates facing strengths from the user's facing parameters. Iterative procedure: enter a trial design (Step 4) and calculate the factor of safety; compare it with the minimum FSOS; modify nail lengths (globally or in selected rows) until it is met; record the maximum load of each nail and take Tmax as the largest; if the nails must be much longer than the range of lengths given in Step 4 (printed 'Step 4e'), increase the drill hole diameter (more cost-effective), decrease the spacing (less cost-effective), or both. Slip surfaces should be investigated above and below the wall, completely behind and beneath the nails, and at each construction stage; complex geometries (multi-tiered walls, sloping terrain above or at the toe) may need general slope stability programs. Input differs by program: some take the pullout resistance as an allowable value (an option in SNAIL or SNAILZ), others bond stress or resistance per unit length; SNAP-2 takes the ultimate (nominal) bond strength. Programs usually report the controlling mechanism (pullout, tensile or facing), so the designer can adjust nail length or hole diameter, bar size, or facing thickness and reinforcement; SNAP-2 reports the layer where pullout occurs. For seismic loading, kh is input (Section 6.8).

Mean soil parameters and mean (nominal) strengths are input

subsections.title: Step 6b Evaluate Global Stability
subsections.summary: Step 6b: global stability by 2D limit-equilibrium ASD analysis with slip surfaces behind the nails, disregarding their contribution. The Owner is responsible in most projects before bid, and analyses may be repeated with the final nail lengths. General slope stability programs are more common than soil nail software, whose slip surfaces may not pass under the toe; stepped walls need compound and long overall slip surfaces (Figure 6.3).
subsections.body: 6.5.2 Step 6b Evaluate Global Stability (pp. 158-159). Global stability must be evaluated with two-dimensional, limit-equilibrium analyses in a conventional ASD framework, with slip surfaces extending behind the soil nails and so disregarding any contribution from the nails. The Owner is responsible for global stability in most projects before construction is put out for bid; depending on the contract, the Contractor may be responsible after bid for verifying internal stability. Because nail lengths are only assumed until the design is complete (by the Owner in Design/Bid/Build or the Contractor in Design/Build), the global analyses may need to be repeated with the final nail lengths. General slope stability programs are more commonly used than dedicated soil nail software (Section 5.6.3): the latter may give reasonable results for simple geometries and regular stratigraphy, but its slip surfaces do not extend under the toe, or the passive resistance below the wall is not modeled correctly; SNAP-2 slip surfaces can extend under the toe, without full user control of trial surfaces. In complex geometries such as the stepped wall of Figure 6.3, internal stability must include compound slip surfaces through some or all of the nails of each wall (dashed lines); all soil nail programs handle short compound surfaces behind individual walls, but only SNAP-2 models compound surfaces below the toe of individual walls, and none properly models the long overall slip surface (filled line).

subsections.title: Step 6c Evaluate Basal Heave (if applicable)
subsections.summary: Step 6c: where soft fine-grained soils exist at the base, basal heave must be evaluated; a high potential may call for another support-of-excavation system. A preliminary check is made in initial design and a detailed one for the final layout, with slope stability programs (slip surfaces under the wall daylighting at the base; undrained short-term conditions more critical) or the simplified method of Section 5.6.6.
subsections.body: 6.5.3 Step 6c Evaluate Basal Heave (if applicable) (pp. 159-160). If soft fine-grained soils exist at the base of a soil nail wall, the potential for heave at the base of the excavation must be evaluated; if computations indicate a high potential, an alternative support-of-excavation system may need to be recommended. A preliminary evaluation should be made during the Initial Design Considerations phase and, if appropriate, a detailed evaluation for the final wall layout. General slope stability programs can in some cases evaluate drained and undrained conditions of the fine-grained soils, with slip surfaces extending under the wall and daylighting at the base of the excavation; for soft fine-grained soils, undrained short-term conditions are more critical than drained conditions. The analysis may require special considerations to force slip surfaces along vertical planes; the simplified method of Section 5.6.6 Basal Heave can be used.
key_points: Evaluate basal heave where soft fine-grained soils exist at the base
High heave potential may require another support-of-excavation system

subsections.title: Step 6d Evaluate Sliding Stability (if applicable)
subsections.summary: Step 6d: sliding along the base of the nail-reinforced block must be evaluated if a horizontal (or unfavorably oriented sub-horizontal) weak layer lies immediately under it. Modern ASD slope stability programs can model planar slip surfaces (most soil nail programs cannot); with them use the Table 5.4 overall stability resistance factors and load factors of 1.0; with the simplified procedure of Section 5.7.7 use the Table 5.7 sliding resistance factors and the Table 5.3 EV and ES load factors.
subsections.body: 6.5.4 Step 6d Evaluate Sliding Stability (if applicable) (p. 160). The potential for sliding along the base of the nail-reinforced block must be evaluated if a horizontal (or sub-horizontal with unfavorable orientation) layer of weak soil is present immediately under the zone of nail-reinforced soil and leads to instability after excavation starts. General, modern ASD slope stability programs can model planar slip surfaces passing along the weak layer, whereas most soil nail design programs cannot model horizontal slip surfaces. If ASD slope stability programs are used, LRFD verifications of sliding should use the resistance factors for overall stability of Table 5.4 and load factors equal to 1.0; if the simplified procedure of Section 5.7.7 Lateral Sliding Stability is used, they should use the sliding resistance factors of Table 5.7 and the EV and ES load factors of Table 5.3.
key_points: Sliding checked where a weak horizontal or sub-horizontal layer underlies the reinforced block
Most soil nail programs cannot model horizontal slip surfaces
ASD slope stability programs: Table 5.4 resistance factors with load factors of 1.0

sections.summary: Step 7 verifies the strength limit states with capacity-to-demand ratios (CDR >= 1.0) and gamma = gammaEV = 1.35: pullout and nail tension on Tmax (7a, 7c), sliding (7b), and facing flexure, punching shear and headed studs on the nail head force To (7d to 7f), plus other facing details (7g).

subsections.title: Overview
subsections.summary: Step 7 starts from the nail loads of the stability analysis: Tmax, the largest, is the load in the LRFD verification of strength limit states, multiplied by gamma = gammaEV = 1.35, the AASHTO (2012) vertical earth load factor, because vertical earth loads matter more than horizontal ones in idealized walls. The factor may need adjustment where surcharges are much larger than earth loads; such loads can be entered in an ASD program multiplied by gamma/gammaEV.
subsections.body: 6.6.1 Overview (pp. 160-161). The designer first obtains from the stability analysis the load at each nail level and selects Tmax as the largest value in all nails; this is the load in the LRFD verification of strength limit states, multiplied by the load factor selected in this manual, gamma = gammaEV = 1.35, where gammaEV is the AASHTO (2012) load factor for vertical earth loads. The factor will be appropriate in most cases: vertical and horizontal earth loads predominate in soil nail walls, and analyses of idealized walls suggest the effect of vertical earth loads is more significant. It may need to be adjusted where surcharge loads are much larger than earth loads. Loads other than soil self-weight (surcharge, traffic) may be considered in an ASD stability program by entering them as adjusted values, the unfactored load multiplied by gamma/gammaEV, where gamma is the load factor associated with that load component.
key_points: Tmax = largest nail load from the stability analysis
Load factor gamma = gammaEV = 1.35 (AASHTO 2012 vertical earth load)
Other loads (surcharge, traffic) entered in an ASD program multiplied by gamma/gammaEV

subsections.title: Step 7a Verify Pullout Resistance
subsections.summary: Step 7a: pullout resistance is mobilized along LP behind the slip surface (read from the program's graphical output). rPO = pi qu DDH (Eq. 6.1); the bond stress is taken as constant along LP for simplicity (Figure 6.4), qu being mobilized at its maximum; RPO = rPO LP (Eq. 6.2); CDR = phiPO RPO / (gamma Tmax) >= 1.0 with gamma = gammaEV = 1.35 (Eq. 6.3).
subsections.body: 6.6.2 Step 7a Verify Pullout Resistance (pp. 161-163). Pullout resistance is mobilized behind the slip surface along the length LP and contributes to overall stability; LP can be estimated from the graphical output of soil nail design programs, where critical slip surfaces and nails are drawn to scale. The nominal (ultimate) pullout resistance per unit length is rPO = pi qu DDH (Eq. 6.1), with qu the bond strength of the nail-grout-soil interface (force per unit area) and DDH the drill hole diameter. Bond stress distributions along the grout-soil interface can be complex and vary along LP (Figure 6.4); for simplicity the distribution is assumed constant along the pullout length, with an apparent average value, and when the bond stress reaches its maximum the bond strength qu is mobilized. The nominal pullout resistance is RPO = rPO LP (Eq. 6.2), and pullout is verified by CDR = phiPO RPO / (gamma Tmax) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.3), with gamma = gammaEV = 1.35 and Tmax the maximum nominal tensile force.
key_points: Eq. 6.1 rPO = pi qu DDH; Eq. 6.2 RPO = rPO LP
Eq. 6.3 CDR = phiPO RPO / (gamma Tmax) >= 1.0, gamma = gammaEV = 1.35

subsections.body: 6.6.3 Step 7b Evaluate Sliding Stability (if applicable) (p. 163). Sliding stability should be evaluated if a layer of weak soil underlies the block of reinforced soil. A simplified hand calculation (Section 5.7.3) can be used when the sliding plane is horizontal; for more complex subsurface conditions a general slope stability program can be used. Sliding stability should be checked with service limit state load factors; minimum factors of safety for the ASD-based analysis are in Table 5.1 for static and seismic cases. In general, soil nail programs cannot model these types of slip surfaces.

subsections.title: Step 7c Verify Nail Tensile Resistance
subsections.summary: Step 7c: CDR = phiT RT / (gamma Tmax) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.4) with RT = At fy (Eq. 6.5). Grade 150 bars reach an apparent yield at 120 ksi and rupture at 150 ksi; Grade 75 bars yield at 75 ksi and rupture at 100 ksi; the grout adds no tensile resistance. Select the smallest bar meeting the required area (Appendix A) and check it suits the hole diameter, corrosion protection plus grout cover, and couplers.
subsections.body: 6.6.4 Step 7c Verify Nail Tensile Resistance (pp. 163-164). The capacity-to-demand ratio is CDR = phiT RT / (gamma Tmax) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.4), with phiT the resistance factor for tensile resistance of the tendon, RT its nominal tensile resistance and gamma the load factor selected for verification. The nominal tensile resistance of the tendon is RT = At fy (Eq. 6.5), with At the tendon cross-sectional area and fy its nominal yield resistance. Grade 150 bars achieve an apparent yield at 120 ksi and a tensile rupture at 150 ksi; Grade 75 bars yield at 75 ksi and rupture at 100 ksi. The grout surrounding the bar does not contribute to the tensile resistance. Select the smallest bar size that meets the required cross-sectional area (Appendix A). Although the Contractor ultimately selects the drill hole diameter, the designer should verify that the tendon diameter is compatible with the estimated hole diameter, the corrosion protection plus grout cover, and couplers.

subsections.title: Step 7d Verify Facing Bending/Flexural Resistance
subsections.summary: Step 7d verifies facing flexure where the program (e.g., SNAP-2) does not: select hi (4 in. typical, or 6), hf (6, 8 typical, 10 in. and thicker for CIP), Grade 60 rebar and WWM, f'c 3,000 to 4,000 psi, bearing plate at least 8 in. x 8 in. x 0.75 in.; reinforcement ratios and areas by Eqs. 6.6-6.8 (Table 6.4, Figure 6.5); bending resistances Eqs. 6.9-6.12; RFF the smaller of Eqs. 6.13 and 6.14 with CF (Table 6.5, Figure 6.6); simplified Eqs. 6.15-6.17 or Table 6.6; CDR = phiFF RFF / (gamma To) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.18).
subsections.body: 6.6.5 Step 7d Verify Facing Bending/Flexural Resistance (pp. 164-171). Initial Calculations (6.6.5a, pp. 164-167): programs like SNAP-2 calculate the flexural resistance and reinforcement ratio checks; otherwise the designer: (1) selects the initial facing thickness hi (4 in. typical, or 6 in.) and final facing thickness hf (6 in., 8 in. typical for final shotcrete, 10 in. and thicker for CIP facing); (2) selects the reinforcement: Grade 60 rebar typically, Grade 60 WWM typical with grades 70, 75 and 80 available, with yield strengths fy_R and fy_W (Appendix A); (3) selects the shotcrete strength f'c, typically 3,000 to 4,000 psi, the latter more common; (4) selects headed studs (Appendix A) and the bearing plate, recommended minimum 8 in. x 8 in. and 0.75 in. thick; (5) calculates the reinforcement ratio rho_ij = [a_ij/(0.5 h)] 100 (Eq. 6.6), where i is v or h and j is n (nail head) or m (mid-span), with a_vn = a_vm + A'VN/SH (Eq. 6.7) and a_hn = a_hm + A'HN/SV (Eq. 6.8), where A'VN = (fy_R/fy_W) AVN and A'HN = (fy_R/fy_W) AHN are equivalent areas for different WWM and rebar yield strengths (Table 6.4: both WWM and rebar contribute at the nail head, only WWM at mid-span; Figure 6.5). The additional rebar in the initial facing is placed near the nail heads, usually within hi of the drill hole; horizontal bars at least 0.60SH long (waler bars equal to SH are common) and vertical bars at least 0.60SV; laps at mid-span; WWM wire spacing per ACI (2011) Section 10.6. Estimation of Nominal Flexural Resistance (6.6.5b, pp. 167-171): RFF is the nail head force when the facing reaches its maximum bending resistance, from the bending capacities around the nails and at mid-span of equivalent two-way slabs; where spacings or reinforcement differ between directions, it is calculated in each direction and the smaller adopted, for both facings. Initial facing: bending resistances m_vm, m_vn, m_hm, m_hn = a f_y_W (hi/2 - a f_y_W/(1.7 f'c)) with the corresponding area (Eqs. 6.9-6.12); RFF is the smaller of CF (m_vm + m_vn)(8 SH/SV) (Eq. 6.13) and CF (m_hm + m_hn)(8 SV/SH) (Eq. 6.14). CF accounts for non-uniform soil pressure, smaller between nails where displacements give stress relief and larger behind the nails (Figure 6.6); Eqs. 6.9-6.14 also apply to the final facing with its own parameters. For Grade 60 WWM and rebar and f'c = 4,000 psi: RFF [kip] = 3.8 CF fy [ksi] F = 228 CF F (Eq. 6.15), with F the smaller of (a_vn + a_vm)(SH h/SV) and (a_hn + a_hm)(SV h/SH) (Eq. 6.16); with equal areas a_s in both directions and SH = SV, RFF [kip] = 456 a_s [in.2/ft] hf [ft] for the final facing, CF = 1.0 (Eq. 6.17). CF (Table 6.5): initial facing 2.0 (4 in.), 1.5 (6 in.), 1.0 (8 in.); final facing 1.0. RFF for the initial facing is calculated with Eqs. 6.15 or 6.17 (as printed), or from Table 6.6 (Grade 60 steel; multiply by 1.24 for Grade 75; divide by 2 for hf = 4 in. and by 1.5 for hf = 6 in.). Final facing: the same steps with its own reinforcement, thickness and materials. Each facing is verified by CDR = phiFF RFF / (gamma To) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.18), with To the maximum nail head force from Eq. 5.1 (Section 5.2.1); if insufficient, increase the facing thickness, the amount or strength of steel, or the concrete strength.

subsections.title: Step 7e Verify Facing Punching Shear Resistance
subsections.summary: Step 7e verifies punching shear at the nail head connection: bearing plate in the initial facing, headed studs in the final facing (Figure 6.7); a conical shear surface forms whose size depends on facing thickness and plate or stud dimensions. CDR = phiFP RFP / (gamma To) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.19); RFP = CP VF (Eq. 6.20), CP = 1.0 (up to 1.15 with soil support); VF = 0.58 sqrt(f'c) pi D'c hc (Eq. 6.21) with D'c and hc by Eqs. 6.22-6.25; or Tables 6.7a and 6.7b. Stud cover at least 2 in.
subsections.body: 6.6.6 Step 7e Verify Facing Punching Shear Resistance (pp. 172-176). Where the program cannot verify punching shear, the designer uses this procedure. Connectors at the nail head may reach a punching shear limit state if the nominal shear resistance of the reinforced shotcrete or concrete around the nails is exceeded; it is evaluated for the initial facing (bearing plate connection) and the final facing (headed stud connection) (Figure 6.7). At the limit state a conical shear surface forms around the nail head, its size governed by the facing thickness and the bearing plate (initial facing) or headed studs (final facing). The nominal resistance must satisfy CDR = phiFP RFP / (gamma To) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.19), with To the maximum nail head force. RFP = CP VF (Eq. 6.20), with CP the factor for soil support under the nail head and VF the basic punching resistance through the facing; CP can be as high as 1.15 if the soil reaction is considered, but the soil support is conservatively taken as negligible, CP = 1.0. VF [kip] = 0.58 sqrt(f'c [psi]) pi D'c [ft] hc [ft] (Eq. 6.21), with D'c the effective equivalent diameter and hc the effective depth of the conical surface, chosen separately for each facing. Initial facing (Figure 6.7a): D'c = LBP + hi (Eq. 6.22) and hc = hi (Eq. 6.23), LBP the bearing plate size. Final facing (Figure 6.7b): D'c = the smaller of SSH + hc and 2 hc (Eq. 6.24), with hc = LS + tP - tSH (Eq. 6.25), SSH the headed stud spacing, LS the stud length, tSH the stud head thickness (Figure 6.8) and tP the bearing plate thickness. LS and hf must give at least 2 in. of final shotcrete or concrete cover over the stud (Section 7.6.7); stud sizes are in Appendix A and manufacturers' references. Simplified method: adopt f'c, facing thickness and LBP, and read RFP from Table 6.7a (initial facing, by hi, f'c and LBP = 8, 9 or 10 in.) and Table 6.7b (final facing, by hc, f'c and SSH = 4, 5 or 6 in.; hc = Ls - tH + tP).

subsections.summary: Step 7f verifies headed studs where the program cannot: RFH = NH AS fy-hs (Eq. 6.26, NH usually 4); CDR = phiFH RFH / (gamma To) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.27); concrete compression behind the studs within limits by AH >= 2.5 AS (Eq. 6.28) and tSH >= 0.5 (DH - DS) (Eq. 6.29); embed the studs beyond mid-facing and behind the WWM; at least 2 in. of cover or per ACI 318; threaded bolts use AE (Eq. 6.30); or Table 6.8.
subsections.body: 6.6.7 Step 7f Verify Facing Headed Stud Resistance (pp. 176-178). For programs that cannot verify headed stud resistance, the designer: (1) computes RFH = NH AS fy-hs (Eq. 6.26), with NH the number of headed studs in the connection (usually 4), AS the cross-sectional area of the stud shaft and fy-hs the stud tensile yield strength; (2) verifies CDR = phiFH RFH / (gamma To) >= 1.0 (Eq. 6.27), with phiFH the resistance factor for headed stud tensile resistance and RFH the nominal tensile resistance of headed studs in final facings; (3) verifies that compression on the concrete behind the studs is within tolerable limits by AH >= 2.5 AS (Eq. 6.28) and tSH >= 0.5 (DH - DS) (Eq. 6.29), with AH the area of the stud head and the head and shaft diameters; (4) provides embedment beyond the middle of the facing section and behind the WWM in the final facing; (5) provides a minimum of 2 in. of cover over connectors, or as suggested by ACI 318, selecting the worst condition; (6) if threaded bolts are used, replaces AS with the effective bolt area AE = (pi/4) [DE - 0.9743/nt]^2 (Eq. 6.30), DE the effective core diameter and nt the threads per unit length. Alternatively, Table 6.8 gives RFH by shaft diameter DSC (3/8 in. 28 kip to 7/8 in. 146 kip, four studs of Grade 60 steel; multiply by 1.24 for Grade 75).

subsections.summary: Step 7g, other facing items: bearing plates of mild steel, minimum Grade 36; heavy-duty hexagonal nuts compatible with the corrosion protection; beveled washers of plain or galvanized steel (spherical seat nuts need none); formal capacity calculations for hardware outside the stated ranges. subsections.body: 6.6.8 Step 7g Other Facing Design Considerations (pp. 178-179). Other items for the facing design: (1) bearing plates of mild steel with minimum Grade 36; (2) heavy-duty, hexagonal nuts at the nail head that include corrosion protection and are compatible with the corrosion protection systems specified by the manufacturers; (3) beveled washers of plain or galvanized steel. If the plate and other hardware are outside the strength and dimension ranges given earlier, a formal calculation of capacities should be performed; some proprietary systems use spherical seat nuts that need no beveled washers. In some permanent walls the initial shotcrete facing also serves as the final facing: the nail head protrudes from the facing and no headed studs are installed. The flexural and punching shear verifications are then required once, with the CF of an initial facing, and no headed stud verification is needed. The engineer designs for a minimum cover of 2 in. on the outside face and 3 in. on the soil side over the reinforcement and nail head elements; long-term protection of the protruding head may be provided with external caps, grease compounds and similar.

subsections.title: Step 8a Evaluate Wall Lateral and Vertical Displacements
subsections.summary: Step 8a: estimate the maximum lateral and vertical displacements behind the wall with the approximate method of Chapter 5 (SNAP-2 lists the limits but does not evaluate deformations). Numerical methods (2D FEM, FDM, plasticity-based models) suit complex geometries, large surcharges or a critical structure within DDEF (Figure 5.16). Lateral movement should be limited to approximately less than 0.3% H for fine-grained soils, 0.2% H for granular soils and 0.1% H for weathered rock and stiff or dense soil; DDEF can reach 1.5H for a vertical wall in fine-grained soils.
subsections.body: 6.7.1 Step 8a Evaluate Wall Lateral and Vertical Displacements (pp. 179-180). A soil nail wall should be designed to limit movements within tolerable ranges. The maximum lateral and vertical displacements of the ground behind the wall are estimated with the approximate method of Chapter 5; these limits are listed in the SNAP-2 output, but the program does not evaluate deformations. For complex geometries or when a critical structure lies within DDEF (Figure 5.16), numerical methods can evaluate the magnitude and distribution of the deflections, most commonly the 2D finite element method (FEM) and the finite difference method (FDM); they may be especially useful where the wall resists relatively large surcharge loads. Plasticity-based soil models should be preferred over elasticity-based models to predict vertical displacement behind the wall; where the excavation drains pore pressures, long-term compression and the ensuing settlement and lateral movement must be considered. The maximum lateral movement should be limited to approximately less than 0.3% H (H = wall height) for fine-grained soils, 0.2% H for granular soils, and 0.1% H for weathered rock and stiff or dense soil. The zone affected by lateral movement extends a distance DDEF that can be up to 1.5 times H for a vertical soil nail wall in fine-grained soils.

subsections.title: Overview
subsections.summary: Soil nail walls have performed much better in earthquakes than gravity structures: surveyed walls showed no significant distress or permanent deflection at accelerations up to 0.7g (Felio et al. 1990; Tatsuoka et al. 1997; Tufenkjian 2002), confirmed by centrifuge tests, owing to flexibility and redundancy. Following AASHTO (2014) Article 11.5.4.2 for MSE walls, seismic design is not mandatory in Seismic Zones 1 to 3 (S1D <= 0.50) or where PGAD <= 0.4g, if the soils do not liquefy or degrade.
subsections.body: 6.8.1 Overview (p. 180). The performance of soil nail walls in earthquakes has historically been much better than that of gravity retaining structures. Observations after recent earthquakes found no significant distress or permanent deflection, although some surveyed walls were subjected to ground accelerations as large as 0.7g (Felio et al. 1990; Tatsuoka et al. 1997; Tufenkjian 2002); Vucetic et al. (1993) and Tufenkjian and Vucetic (2000) observed similar trends in centrifuge tests on reduced-scale models. The satisfactory performance is attributed to flexibility and design redundancy. Soil nail walls still need to be fully designed for seismic loads when applicable. AASHTO (2014) Article 11.5.4.2 gives guidance on when earth-retaining structures need analysis at the Extreme-Event I limit state; its criteria for MSE walls, another flexible system, can be considered appropriate for soil nail walls: seismic design is not mandatory in Seismic Zone 1 (S1D <= 0.15), Zone 2 (0.15 < S1D <= 0.30) and Zone 3 (0.30 < S1D <= 0.50), or at sites where the site-adjusted design PGAD is <= 0.4g, as long as the soils behind the wall do not liquefy (mainly cohesionless soils) or sustain significant strength degradation (mainly fine-grained soils). Where seismic analyses are needed, the steps that follow, based on Kavazanjian et al. (2011), are recommended.
key_points: No significant distress observed at ground accelerations up to 0.7g

subsections.title: Step 9a Select Design Seismic Parameters
subsections.summary: Step 9a: obtain PGA and S1 from AASHTO (2014) for a 1,000-year return period and Site Class B (Section 4.9); determine the average shear-wave velocity, N60 or Su in the upper 100 ft (from the planned top of wall); assign the Site Class (Table 4.8); obtain FPGA and Fv (Tables 4.9, 4.10) for Site Classes A to E (site-specific analysis for F); PGAD = FPGA PGA and SD1 = Fv S1; kmax = PGAD for Site Classes C to E (Eq. 6.31), 1.2 PGAD for A and B (Eq. 6.32).
subsections.body: 6.8.2 Step 9a Select Design Seismic Parameters (p. 181). (1) Obtain the seismic parameters (PGA and S1) from AASHTO (2014) for a 1,000-year return period for reference Site Class B (Section 4.9), or another return period if required by the Owner. (2) Determine the average shear-wave velocity, average N60 or average Su (cohesive soils) in the upper 100 ft, considered from the planned top of wall. (3) Assign a Site Class (A through F) using Table 4.8. (4) For Site Classes A to E obtain the site modification factors FPGA and Fv from Tables 4.9 and 4.10; for Site Class F perform a site-specific response analysis (beyond the scope of the manual; Kavazanjian et al. 2011). (5) Calculate the design, site-corrected peak ground acceleration and 1-sec response acceleration: PGAD = FPGA PGA and SD1 = Fv S1. (6) Determine the maximum seismic coefficient kmax, the basis for input in the limit-equilibrium analysis: kmax = PGAD for Site Classes C through E (Eq. 6.31), and kmax = 1.2 PGAD for Site Classes A and B (Eq. 6.32), which are not typical conditions for soil nail walls.

subsections.title: Step 9b Adjustment of Design Seismic Coefficients
subsections.summary: Step 9b: for walls 20 ft high or more, kh = alpha kmax (Eq. 6.33), alpha = 1 + 0.01 H (0.5 beta - 1) (Eq. 6.34), beta = S1D/kmax. Deformations of flexible walls tend to be small for 0.5 <= kh/PGA <= 0.67. Tolerable movement categories: rigid; about 1 to 2 in.; more than 2 in. Displacement de by Eq. 6.35 (Newmark type sliding block), ky giving FSOS = 1.0, PGV = 38 SD1. Then kh = kmax (rigid, Eq. 6.36), 0.5 kmax (1-2 in., Eq. 6.37) or r kmax (more than 2 in., Eq. 6.38), r = ky/kmax (Eq. 6.39).
subsections.body: 6.8.3 Step 9b Adjustment of Design Seismic Coefficients (pp. 181-184). Wall height: if the wall is 20 ft high or more, kmax can be reduced to account for the decrease of seismic wave intensity as waves propagate from the base to the top of the wall (wave scattering or spatial incoherence over a longer path); the adjustment averages the intensity over the wall height. The adjusted value is the seismic coefficient kh = alpha kmax (Eq. 6.33), with alpha = 1 + 0.01 H (0.5 beta - 1) (Eq. 6.34), H the wall height and beta = S1D/kmax. Seismic deformations: soil nail walls are more flexible than gravity walls and can tolerate some lateral displacement; permanent deformations of relatively flexible walls tend to be small when 0.5 <= kh/PGA <= 0.67, as long as the soil strength does not drop significantly in strong shaking. First assess whether the wall can accept permanent movements; categories (Kavazanjian et al. 2011): rigid systems unable to sustain permanent displacement (structural features or an adjacent deformation-sensitive structure); systems able to sustain approximately 1 to 2 in.; systems able to sustain more than 2 in. Next estimate the permanent displacement, analogous to the Newmark (1965) sliding block method (details in Kavazanjian et al. 2011), simplified as Eq. 6.35, log(de) = -1.51 - 0.74 log(ky/kmax) + 3.27 log(1 - ky/kmax) - 0.80 kmax + 1.59 PGV, with ky the yield acceleration from the overall stability analysis (the seismic coefficient giving FSOS = 1.0, found with the limit-equilibrium program during static design) and PGV = 38 SD1. Finally: rigid walls kh = kmax (Eq. 6.36); walls able to sustain 1-2 in., kh = 0.5 kmax (Eq. 6.37); walls able to sustain more than 2 in., kh = r kmax (Eq. 6.38), with the ductility reduction factor r = ky/kmax (Eq. 6.39); r = 1.0 can be considered for rigid walls and r = 0.5 for walls able to sustain more than 2 in.

subsections.title: Alternative Evaluation of Seismic Effects on Overall Stability
subsections.summary: The Mononobe-Okabe method, an extension of Coulomb theory, may be used as an alternative despite its limitations: rigid block, active pressures, cohesionless soils, no pore pressures; pseudo-static forces kh W and kv W act at the wedge centroid (Figure 6.9), the vertical component disregarded. PAE = (gamma_s H^2/2) KAE (1 - kv) (Eq. 6.40), KAE by Eqs. 6.41-6.43 or Figure 6.10 (phi 20 to 45 degrees, kv = 0, delta = 0.75 phi); apparent cohesion limited by Table 6.9 (NCHRP 2008), its effect in Figure 6.11.
subsections.body: 6.8.5 Alternative Evaluation of Seismic Effects on Overall Stability (pp. 184-188). The most commonly used pseudo-static procedure has been the Mononobe-Okabe method, an extension of Coulomb theory (Mononobe 1929; Okabe 1926); it may be used as an alternative method for the seismic stability of soil nail walls despite its limitations (Kavazanjian et al. 2011), because it is simple and gives acceptable results for certain conditions. Described by Seed and Whitman (1970), Richards and Elms (1979) and Kavazanjian et al. (2011), it was developed for gravity walls and assumes that the wall and soil behind it act as a rigid block, active earth pressures develop, the soils are cohesionless, and no pore pressures develop. Inertial forces are taken as equivalent pseudo-static forces at the centroid of the potentially unstable block (Figure 6.9): kh W horizontally and kv W vertically, W the wedge weight; the vertical component is disregarded. The total active thrust is PAE = (gamma_s H^2/2) KAE (1 - kv) (Eq. 6.40; Ebeling and Morrison 1992; Kavazanjian et al. 2011), with gamma_s the unit weight of soil behind the wall, H the wall height and KAE the active pressure coefficient. With sloping ground behind the wall, KAE = cos^2(phi_f - omega - alpha') / [cos omega cos^2 alpha' cos(alpha' + delta + omega) D] (Eq. 6.41), with phi_f the soil friction angle, alpha' the batter of the wall internal face from vertical, beta the backslope angle, delta the wall-soil interface friction angle, omega = tan^-1[kh/(1 - kv)] (Eq. 6.42), and D = [1 + sqrt(sin(phi_f + delta) sin(phi_f - omega - beta) / (cos(delta + alpha' + omega) cos(beta - alpha')))]^2 (Eq. 6.43). The slip plane lies at an angle xi that can be much flatter than for static conditions (Zarrabi-Kashani 1979; Kramer 1996; Kavazanjian et al. 2011). KAE can also be read from Figure 6.10: (a) KAE against kh for phi from 20 to 45 degrees with a horizontal backslope, kv = 0 and delta = 0.75 phi; (b) a correction factor for a non-horizontal backslope. The formulation gives no solution for increasing backslope angles or seismic coefficients; alternatives are in NCHRP (2008). Cohesion, not considered originally, can significantly reduce KAE (NCHRP 2008; Kavazanjian et al. 2011); the apparent cohesion included is limited by Table 6.9 (5-15 percent passing No. 200, 50 psf; 15-25 percent, 100 psf; 25-50 percent, 200 psf). Figure 6.11 shows corrected KAE against c/(gamma_s H) for phi = 35 degrees and beta = 0; NCHRP (2008) gives plots for 30 to 40 degrees.

subsections.title: Introduction
subsections.summary: Step 10: the designer must provide adequate subsurface and surface drainage unless it is not needed. Facings are lightly loaded and lightly reinforced and not designed for hydrostatic forces; incidental water is assumed handled by the strip drains. Uncontrolled water causes construction difficulties, cost and delay, loss of long-term integrity, poor performance and aesthetics; walls perform significantly better with effective drainage (Chapter 3).
subsections.body: 6.9.1 Introduction (pp. 188-189). The design engineer must provide adequate subsurface and surface drainage features in all walls unless they are determined not to be needed for a specific project. Soil nail wall facings are assumed relatively lightly loaded and therefore lightly reinforced, and are not designed to resist hydrostatic forces; incidental water behind the face is assumed to be handled by the strip drains. Uncontrolled surface runoff or groundwater can cause construction difficulties, increase construction cost and duration, impair long-term integrity, negatively affect performance and degrade aesthetics, so both must be controlled during and after construction; soil nail walls perform significantly better with an effective drainage system. Drainage systems are discussed in Chapter 3; this section covers design and constructability considerations.

subsections.title: Short-Term Surface Water and Groundwater Control
subsections.summary: Short-term control during construction covers at least surface runoff and perched or localized seepage: a concrete-lined interceptor ditch along the crest, applied with the first lift's shotcrete, is often used, but is unnecessary where the ground slopes away or runoff is small; wells or well points beyond the nail length may handle perched water, though nailing may then not be cost-effective. Temporary water control is the Contractor's responsibility, informed by the Owner's exploration.
subsections.body: 6.9.2 Short-Term Surface Water and Groundwater Control (p. 189). Dewatering during construction includes, at a minimum, control of surface runoff and of subsurface flow from perched water or localized seepage. A surface water interceptor ditch, excavated along the crest of the excavation and lined with concrete applied during shotcreting of the first lift, is often used to control runoff toward the face and limit infiltration into the retained soil; diverted flow over the face may cause erosion and localized instability before the initial facing is built. Ditches must have suitable slopes for positive drainage away from the excavation, since improper ditches create erosion, ponding or infiltration; a ditch is generally unnecessary if the area above the wall slopes away from the face or the potential for significant runoff or infiltration is small. Where significant seepage from perched water is expected, wells or well points may be installed for temporary dewatering, typically beyond the length of the nails to avoid damage during drilling; wells add cost, and soil nailing might then not be cost-effective. Temporary control of surface runoff, ponding, infiltration and groundwater is the Contractor's responsibility, conveying water away by gravity or sump pumps; if the Owner performs the exploration, enough information should be collected in design to identify the need for drainage and help the Contractor select and size drainage and dewatering elements.
key_points: Concrete-lined interceptor ditch along the crest, placed with the first lift's shotcrete
Ditch unnecessary where the ground slopes away from the wall or runoff is small
Wells or well points for perched water, installed beyond the nail length
Temporary water control is the Contractor's responsibility

subsections.title: Long-Term Surface Water and Groundwater Control
subsections.summary: Long-term control. Low groundwater: strip drains by judgment, spaced 1.0 SH to 2.0 SH (SH most common); weepholes 2- to 4-in. PVC, 12 to 16 in. long, 8 to 10 ft apart along the base with a filter plug of at least 1 ft3; or an underdrain with a Schedule 40 PVC toe drain in geotextile-wrapped aggregate. High groundwater: seepage analysis, groundwater kept at least 2 ft below the nails and facing base, drain pipes (2-in. slotted PVC at 5 to 10 degrees, about one per 100 ft2). Permanent surface control: an interception ditch behind the wall.
subsections.body: 6.9.3 Long-Term Surface Water and Groundwater Control (pp. 190-193). Control for Low Groundwater or Low Volumes of Seepage (6.9.3a, pp. 190-191): seepage calculations are often not needed for strip drains; the designer specifies the type and spacing by judgment and experience, typically 1.0 SH to 2.0 SH, with SH more common; too close a spacing reduces soil-shotcrete contact and may cause sloughing; commercial widths must be considered. Weepholes, sized and spaced by experience, are typically 2- to 4-in. diameter PVC pipes 12 to 16 in. long (depending on the facing thickness), spaced 8 to 10 ft along the base, backed with geotextile and a filter plug of at least 1 ft3 of filter aggregate wrapped in geotextile; they are also placed at localized seepage, and surface flow in front of the wall and freezing may need consideration. Alternatively an underdrain system connects the strips through short pipes to a toe drain parallel to the toe: Schedule 40 PVC solid and slotted pipe in clean, coarse, gravel-sized aggregate free of fines, the aggregate trench wrapped in geotextile filter fabric (geotextile directly over the slotted pipe must be avoided) meeting filter criteria (Holtz et al. 2008). Schematic details are in Figures 6.12 and 6.13 (some impractical in places, e.g., a concrete ditch in steep terrain). On highly irregular faces the strip drains may be installed between the initial and final facings, with holes drilled through the initial facing. Control for High Groundwater (6.9.3b, pp. 191-192): where groundwater must be permanently lowered, perform seepage analyses for the flow rate behind the wall and select strips by flow rate, permittivity and acceptable heads; use a redundant or over-sized system; aim to keep groundwater at least 2 ft below the nails and the base of the facing at all times, or evaluate elevated groundwater for internal and global stability, facing pressures and corrosion. Where strips are not sufficient, drain pipes are installed horizontally or with a mild upslope (5 to 10 degrees) to reduce pore pressures (Figure 6.12); they are 2-in. diameter slotted or perforated PVC tubes exiting through the face (Figure 6.13), larger or in several rows if seepage analysis requires; 1 to 3 ft long for shallow or perched water, longer for high groundwater; commonly about one per 100 ft2 of face; plugged or capped during shotcreting. They need long-term maintenance, and clogging raises water pressure and reduces overall, sliding and internal stability. Permanent Surface Water Control (6.9.3c, p. 192): an interception ditch behind the wall prevents runoff infiltrating behind the wall or flowing over its edge.

Weepholes: 2- to 4-in. PVC, 12 to 16 in. long, 8 to 10 ft apart along the base, with at least 1 ft3 filter plug
Underdrain alternative: Schedule 40 PVC toe drain in clean aggregate wrapped in geotextile (not geotextile on the pipe)
High groundwater: seepage analysis; keep water at least 2 ft below the nails and the facing base
Drain pipes: 2-in. slotted or perforated PVC at 5 to 10 degrees upslope, 1 to 3 ft or longer, about one per 100 ft2 of face
Drain pipes need long-term maintenance; clogging reduces stability
Permanent interception ditch behind the wall

sections.title: Specialty Items
sections.summary: Specialty items: stepped walls (shorter nails than a non-stepped wall of the same height; independent tiers when the setback exceeds the lower wall height), composite walls (mostly soil nails with ground anchors; design the nails for shallow surfaces and the anchors for deeper ones, GEC 4), strut-nails (steep bars near the excavation base, acting in compression, that support the facing vertically, designed like micropiles), and frost protection (porous backfill, thicker facing, larger tendons, insulation; north-facing walls 1.4 to 2 times the frost depth of south-facing).
sections.body: 6.10 Specialty Items (pp. 194-202). Subsections 6.10.1 Stepped Walls to 6.10.4 Considerations for Frost Protection.

subsections.title: Stepped Walls
subsections.summary: Stepped walls (two or more walls with setbacks, Figure 6.14) need shorter nails than a full-height wall of the same height but are less frequent on transportation projects; they suit cheap excavation and expensive nailing, or sites where global instability or heave rules out a full-height wall. A setback under about 1/20 of the combined height acts as a battered wall (about 3 degrees); a setback larger than the lower wall height H2 makes the walls independent; otherwise the lower wall is analyzed with the upper one. The bench must be sloped and lined.
subsections.body: 6.10.1 Stepped Walls (pp. 194-195). Stepped or benched walls consist of two or more soil nail walls with vertical or battered faces and horizontal setbacks between them (Figure 6.14); the section discusses the most common two-tier wall with vertical faces, applicable to any number of tiers. Stepped walls generally require shorter nails than non-stepped walls of the same total height, but are less frequently constructed on transportation projects; they may save cost where extra excavation is cheap and nailing relatively expensive. Where overall stability controls, a full-height wall may need long nails with large resistance, and global instability or bottom heave may make a full-height wall impossible; stepped walls with a relatively wide setback may then be used, and planters between the walls can add aesthetic value. Stepped or battered walls can solve similar problems. A stepped wall acts as an equivalent battered wall when the setback is small: following MSE wall guidance, when it is less than about 1/20 of the combined height (an equivalent batter of 3 degrees). When the setback is larger than the height of the lower wall (H2), the internal stability of each wall is independent and they can be analyzed separately; when smaller, the lower wall must be analyzed considering the upper wall, e.g., an upper MSE wall modeled in a soil nail program as vertical surcharge and shear forces (a likely conservative simplification whose slip surfaces may not match MSE design), or more accurately both walls and reinforcements in a general slope stability program. Surface drainage of the bench must avoid ponding and infiltration into the lower wall: the bench is sloped and lined as needed, and sprinkler water must be considered if planted.
key_points: Stepped walls need shorter nails than non-stepped walls of the same height; less frequent on transportation projects
Setback < about 1/20 of combined height acts as a battered wall (about 3 degrees)
Setback > lower wall height H2: walls independent; otherwise analyze the lower wall with the upper one
Upper MSE wall as surcharge and shear (conservative) or both walls in a general slope stability program
Bench sloped and lined to avoid ponding and infiltration

subsections.title: Composite Walls
subsections.summary: Composite walls are typically soil nails with ground anchors (Figure 6.15), installed top-down. Anchors near the top to control movement are rare; they cannot usually be tensioned against initial shotcrete without bearing pads or a thicker facing, and their vertical component matters, especially above 20 degrees. More commonly anchors address global instability, preferably near the bottom and tensioned after the final facing, or full height with concrete posts. Design: analyze the nails only for slip surfaces within 1.5 nail lengths behind the top, treat the nailed zone as a rigid block, and size the anchors for deeper surfaces (GEC No. 4).
subsections.body: 6.10.2 Composite Walls (pp. 196-198). The most typical composite wall combines a soil nail wall with ground anchors (Figure 6.15), both installed as excavation proceeds from top to bottom. Anchors near the top (Figure 6.15a) could control ground movement above the wall, but this is relatively rare: most structures and utilities tolerate the movements, which can otherwise be reduced with stiffer nails of larger section or by underpinning; one case is a very deep excavation next to a settlement-sensitive structure where underpinning is impractical, or where the structure applies horizontal forces the nails cannot counter. Anchors cannot typically be tensioned against the initial shotcrete facing (punching shear and bending), so bearing pads or a thicker, more reinforced initial facing are needed, and the Owner must consider space limitations in the project documents. Because anchors are inclined, the stability of the wall under their vertical component during excavation of later lifts must be considered, especially above 20 degrees from horizontal; excavation in a checkerboard pattern or vertical micropiles below the excavation base can mitigate it. Anchors are more commonly added where global instability would be impractical to address with nails; if not needed for temporary stability they are preferably installed near the bottom and tensioned after the final facing; where many are needed, along the full height with cast-in-situ or precast concrete posts (Figure 6.15b), the nailed sections acting as lagging, in which case an all-anchor solution may be more practical. Because nails and anchors address different limit states, the wall is analyzed with nails only, limiting slip surfaces to shallow ones no further behind the top than 1.5 times the nail length; the nailed zone is then a rigid block and the anchors provide stability against deeper surfaces, which controls their length (GEC No. 4, Sabatini et al. 1999); only a few soil nail programs can include anchors. Hybrid soil nail/MSE walls (Figure 2.6, Chapter 2) can be designed with soil nail programs.

Anchors cannot usually be tensioned against initial shotcrete without bearing pads or a thicker facing
Consider the anchors' vertical component, especially above 20 degrees
Anchors for global instability: preferably near the bottom, tensioned after the final facing

subsections.title: Strut-Nails
subsections.summary: Strut-nails (toe-nails) are drilled and grouted bars at steep angles (up to about 15 or 20 degrees to 45 degrees from vertical) near the excavation base that support the facing vertically (Figure 6.16); short, in compression, like Case I micropiles and designed with micropile procedures (Sabatini et al. 2005) by equilibrium of W, CST and TT, TT being added to the nail above. Check the added facing moment and buckling. Applications: temporary lift support (uncommon), vertical elements at 2 to 3 ft in poor soils, and, typically, support of the final facing where the wall ends at bedrock.
subsections.body: 6.10.3 Strut-Nails (pp. 198-200). Overview (6.10.3a, pp. 198-200): strut-nails or toe-nails are drilled and grouted bars installed at steep angles (up to about 15 or 20 degrees to 45 degrees from the vertical) near the bottom of the excavation to give the facing vertical support (Figure 6.16), used when the facing weight or uncommon heavy loads at its top are large and the soils below the wall cannot provide the bearing. They are relatively short (a fraction of the wall height), act in compression, connect to the wall with a bearing plate and washers, and resemble Case I micropiles; micropile design procedures (Sabatini et al. 2005) apply. Design is by force equilibrium, by hand after the regular nails are designed, with the facing weight W, the strut-nail compression CST and the tension TT in the nail immediately above: the vertical component of CST equals W plus the vertical component of TT. TT must be added to the axial load T of that nail head from conventional design, which may require a larger nail. Vertical components of the nails above are assumed carried by facing-soil friction, which is invalid if those nails are significantly inclined. The opposing horizontal components of TT and CST create a bending moment in the facing between the strut-nail and the nail above, maximum at that nail and additive to the conventional moments; it decreases as the strut-nail is placed closer to the nail above, so strut-nails should be installed close to, or staggered within, the bottom row. Buckling may occur if strut-nails are too close to the face or poorly confined; it is evaluated as for micropiles, and a stub casing in the upper few feet can increase resistance. Applications (6.10.3b, p. 200): temporary support of the facing of a lift left unsupported by the next excavation is not common, since nails support 4-in. shotcrete and, in competent ground, up to 8 to 10 in.; thicker facings should be evaluated formally. Hollow or solid bars installed vertically along the alignment, extending below final grade at a spacing of about 2 to 3 ft, give lateral support to each lift and vertical support to the facing in soils not conducive to nailing. More typically, strut-nails support the final facing in difficult subgrades, e.g., where a wall supporting a soil-and-rock cut ends at or slightly below top of bedrock, with strut-nails at the toe extending into the rock.
key_points: Strut-nails: steep (about 15-20 to 45 degrees from vertical), short, in compression, vertical support of the facing
Designed like Case I micropiles (Sabatini et al. 2005) by equilibrium of W, CST and TT
TT is added to the axial load of the nail above
Opposing horizontal components add facing bending; install close to or staggered within the bottom row
Check buckling as for micropiles; a stub casing increases resistance
Typical use: final facing support where the wall ends at bedrock; vertical elements at about 2 to 3 ft in poor soils

subsections.title: Considerations for Frost Protection
subsections.summary: Soil nail walls are always susceptible to frost because of the exposed facing, so frost-susceptible soils need protection and conservative design: porous backfill against moisture build-up, a facing slightly thicker than the frost depth, larger tendons, and insulation (Figure 6.17), e.g., EPS foam panels (1 in. considered thermally equivalent to 1 ft of gravel), selected by R-value. North-facing walls may have 1.4 to 2 times the frost penetration of south-facing walls; drain the ground above the wall.
subsections.body: 6.10.4 Considerations for Frost Protection (pp. 201-202). Unlike foundations placed below the frost penetration depth, soil nail walls are always susceptible to frost effects because of the exposed facing, so walls in frost-susceptible soils need frost protection. Design for frost-induced nail loads must be conservative because data are limited; the engineer would consider: (i) preventing moisture build-up behind the wall with porous backfill (e.g., gravel); (ii) a facing slightly thicker than the frost depth; (iii) larger tendons; and (iv) insulation on the wall face. Thermal insulation (Figure 6.17) can be extruded polystyrene (EPS) foam panels, lightweight and cost-effective: a 1-in. thick panel is considered thermally equivalent to a 1-ft thick layer of gravel. Thickness is selected by the thermal resistance (R-value), the ratio of the temperature drop across the material to the heat transferred per unit area and time for a given thickness, proportional to thickness; higher R-values insulate better; detailed thermal design is beyond the manual's scope. Wall orientation matters: north-facing walls may have 1.4 to 2 times the frost penetration of south-facing walls exposed to sunlight. Drainage of the ground above the wall decreases infiltration and frost potential.

Porous backfill, facing slightly thicker than the frost depth, larger tendons, insulation
1 in. of EPS foam considered thermally equivalent to 1 ft of gravel; select by R-value
North-facing walls may have 1.4 to 2 times the frost penetration of south-facing walls

sections.title: Step 11 Other Design Considerations
sections.summary: Step 11: final constructability evaluations where the design has special construction needs (temporary support of exposed lifts, strut-nails); a load testing program to verify the assumed design values, which the Owner's design engineer will always have to develop (Chapter 9); and, where needed, a geotechnical monitoring plan for wall deformations during and after construction.
sections.body: 6.11 Step 11 Other Design Considerations (p. 203). Final evaluations of constructability may need to be carried out if the design has requirements for special construction needs, such as temporary support of exposed lifts or use of strut-nails. The Owner's design engineer will always have to develop a load testing program to verify the assumed design values; recommendations are in Chapter 9. The Owner's design engineer may also need to prepare a geotechnical monitoring plan specifying how wall deformations will be evaluated during and after construction. As printed, such a plan would only be needed if the wall deformations were found to be "non-significant" during design (the sense of the passage suggests significant), or if a deformation-sensitive structure near the wall was considered a risk to the project.
key_points: Final constructability evaluation for special needs (temporary support of exposed lifts, strut-nails)
Owner's design engineer always develops a load testing program to verify design values (Chapter 9)
Geotechnical monitoring plan where deformations matter or a deformation-sensitive structure is near the wall

subsections.title: Pre-Construction
subsections.summary: In Design/Bid/Build contracts, the drawings and specifications are best overseen by the people who did the design, so the design intent is conveyed unambiguously; their preparation is part of the Design phase. Pre-construction covers the Owner's engineering cost estimate, evaluation of bidders' experience and selection of the contractor (Chapter 8).
subsections.body: 6.12.1 Pre-Construction (p. 203). In Design/Bid/Build contracts, oversight of the preparation of construction drawings and specifications by the same personnel performing the design is highly desirable, to ensure the design intent is unambiguously conveyed; drawing and specification preparation should be an integral part of the Design phase. The Pre-Construction phase includes the preparation of the Owner's engineering cost estimates, the evaluation of bidders' experience, and the selection of the contractor. Chapter 8 Contracting Approaches and Specifications gives guidelines for these activities.
key_points: Design/Bid/Build: drawings and specifications overseen by the designers, as part of the Design phase
Pre-construction: Owner's cost estimate, evaluation of bidders' experience, contractor selection (Chapter 8)

subsections.title: Construction and Post-Construction
subsections.summary: Construction and post-construction activities: evaluation of the Contractor's submittals; observation and evaluation of load testing (part of construction quality assurance), of construction methods and of production nail installation; observation of drainage and facing construction; geotechnical monitoring during construction and/or long term; and post-construction engineering reports (Chapter 9).
subsections.body: 6.12.2 Construction and Post-Construction (pp. 203-204). The Construction and Post-Construction phases include: evaluation of the Contractor's submittals; observation and evaluation of load testing (as part of construction quality assurance); observation and evaluation of construction methods; observation and evaluation of the installation of production nails; observation of drainage and facing construction; geotechnical monitoring during construction and/or in the long term; and preparation of post-construction engineering reports. Chapter 9 Construction Inspection and Performance Monitoring gives guidelines for the main technical activities during and after construction.
key_points: Submittal review, load testing observation (QA), construction methods, production nails
Drainage and facing observation, geotechnical monitoring, post-construction reports (Chapter 9)
